correctness.rationale: Baronti–Bertella Definition 3 gives exactly the stated \(H_2\) quotient, and their Proposition 4 permits reduction to \(0<\lambda\le1\) after swapping the ordered pair. Balestro–Martini–Teixeira Theorem 4.1 classifies every unit isosceles-orthogonal pair in a symmetric plane as quarter-turn partners up to sign. With \(\lambda=\tan\theta\), the quotient becomes the reciprocal norm of a coordinate rotation, whose supremum is the inverse-rotation operator norm. For a regular \(4n\)-gon, convexity reduces the rotation operator norm to a vertex and support-normal geometry gives \(\cos d/\cos(\pi/(4n))\le\sec(\pi/(4n))\), with equality at \(\theta=\pi/(4n)\). The explicit axes pair attains the bound.
risks: The symmetric-plane classification is a cited nonstandard lemma rather than reproved from first principles; its full statement and hypotheses were inspected.
No computation is used to bridge from finitely many examples to the all-n formula.

value.rationale: The result does more than tabulate one polygon: it identifies the quadratic isosceles constant of every symmetric plane with a concrete rotation-distortion profile. The affine regular \(4n\)-gons then form a canonical infinite benchmark family with the exact law \(\sec(\pi/(4n))\), ranging from the square endpoint \(\sqrt2\) down to the Hilbert value \(1\). This gives a structural interpretation of the newly introduced invariant and a reusable method for other symmetric norms.
risks: The closed-form polygon corollary uses strong rotational symmetry and does not automatically extend to arbitrary centrally symmetric polygons.
